definition: Coronation means the formal ceremony in which a new king or queen is invested with royal authority.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word coronation. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know coronation should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Crowds pressed against the palace gates for the coronation, waiting hours to glimpse the new queen as she was handed the scepter and orb.
An accession proclamation merely announces that a new sovereign has succeeded — a herald's declaration, with none of the sacred ritual a coronation carries.
An enthronement formally seats the ruler on the throne, but a coronation goes further, crowning the monarch with the full regalia and investing complete royal authority.

Crowning names the physical act itself — the moment the crown is set on the monarch's head. Coronation means the entire formal ceremony built around that gesture: the oaths, the anointing, the regalia, and the whole legal and religious rite.

An investiture formally confers any office or authority along with its insignia — a knight, a bishop, or a chancellor can each receive one. A coronation is narrower: it is specifically the investiture of a monarch, centered on the crown.

Installation is the general term for formally placing anyone in an office or post — a judge, a dean, a board chair. A coronation is one specific, royal kind of installation: the rite that crowns a monarch and grants full royal authority.
The formal act of giving up royal authority and stepping down from the throne — a coronation begins a reign; an abdication ends it.
The removal of a monarch from the throne, often by force — where a coronation installs a ruler, dethronement strips one of power.

A coronation is not just a party, a broadcast, or a grand public occasion — it is the formal ceremony in which a new monarch is invested with royal authority.
Looser words like "celebration" or "ceremony" tell you only that something festive or ritual is taking place; they do not specify that a king or queen is being granted the legal right to rule.

The concerts, parades, and street parties around the event were celebrations, and the televised pageantry was a ceremony — but the coronation was the one act that actually transferred sovereign power.
Reach for "coronation" only when the point is the official investiture of a monarch, not merely the festivities surrounding it.
formal, dignified, and historical
"coronation" is a formal noun tied to monarchy, history, and journalism, so it fits ceremonial, news, or scholarly writing.
Keep it for the literal crowning of a king or queen.
Using it loosely for any big promotion or triumph — "his coronation as CEO" — is figurative and can sound grandiose or lightly ironic, so choose that extended sense deliberately.

Medieval kings often waited months to hold a coronation, and the delay was strategy, not laziness.
A dead king's heir ruled at once in law.
But ruling and being seen to rule were different things, and the great ceremony existed to close that gap.
Every element was staged for witnesses: nobles swearing loyalty aloud, holy oil on the new king's brow, the regalia carried through the crowd piece by piece.
Chronicles rarely dwell on the moment the crown touched the head.
They describe the oaths, the anointing, and who stood where -- the machinery of consent.
A wise heir therefore waited until rivals could attend and be seen kneeling.
The rite mattered most as a public act witnessed by the whole realm.
